output.methodChoice: D (competing hypotheses) with K-T style IS/IS NOT comparison: the question is which rival explains the gap, and a confounder (time in level) is the key.
output.brief: The gap is mostly a difference in who is eligible, not where people work. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level that policy requires, versus 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, and the observed rate is 7.6%. The by-job-family breakdown doesn't change this, because tenure differs within every family. I can't confirm proximity bias. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real gap of a few points can't be ruled out. Staffing data can't show who gets stretch work, and I haven't tested attrition. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It rests on an unsupported diagnosis, and it would hit about 180 people hired on home-based contracts. Instead, change promotion reporting to compare eligible employees only, and re-check it at FY2027. Meanwhile, begin tracking stretch assignments, and explain eligibility rules to remote staff. Confidence is moderate to high.
